md_docs_2crypto-policy(3) Library Functions Manual md_docs_2crypto-policy(3)

NAME

md_docs_2crypto-policy - Connection security policy

Native clients and the browser use crypto_policy_resolve() from include/ascii-chat/crypto/policy.h. Mobile clients should call this same API. Its result is the existing ACIP mode bitmask: NONE (0), ENCRYPT (1), AUTH (2), or FULL (3). Authentication and payload encryption are independent.

Input Plain TCP / WS TLS / WSS / WebRTC DTLS Default, no credentials ENCRYPT NONE Password FULL FULL Identity key or pinned server key FULL AUTH Explicit encryption ENCRYPT ENCRYPT Key and explicit no-encrypt AUTH AUTH Password and explicit no-encrypt AUTH AUTH No-auth, no credentials ENCRYPT NONE No-auth and no-encrypt NONE NONE

An explicit encryption setting takes precedence over transport/password defaults. Supplying both encrypt and no-encrypt is an error. Supplying authentication material with no-auth is an error. Keys alone do not force a second encryption layer over TLS or DTLS. Config files, environment variables, and CLI flags retain that precedence: an enabled higher-priority encryption choice overrides the opposite lower-priority choice. Contradictory choices in the same layer are rejected.

For example, both peers can authenticate identities without ACIP payload encryption:

ascii-chat server --key server_key --client-keys client_key.pub --no-encrypt
ascii-chat client localhost --key client_key --server-key server_key.pub --no-encrypt

On plain transports the server must explicitly permit unencrypted payloads with --no-encrypt. A TLS listener permits TLS-only connections by default, but configured passwords or client allowlists still require authentication. Server --encrypt requires ACIP encryption; server --no-encrypt requires ACIP plaintext. Neither flag disables identity loading or signature checks.

Direct TCP and WebSocket clients begin with PROTOCOL_VERSION and the resolved mode. The server validates its requirements and echoes that mode. Nonzero modes continue through capability negotiation, key exchange and authentication. Application packets are sent only after negotiation succeeds. AUTH retains the completed crypto context for identity state while transports omit ENCRYPTED wrappers. WSS continues to encrypt those packets with TLS.

The browser passes its optional encryption override and configured credentials to WASM. JavaScript does not implement another policy decision table. Its connection state waits for authentication even when payload encryption is off. WebRTC always retains DTLS and negotiates the same policy independently for each media peer using acip_security_t. Passwords or explicit encryption add ACIP ENCRYPTED envelopes; auth-only verifies credentials without those envelopes. Media is admitted only after peer negotiation succeeds. Discovery signaling has its own credentials and security context. Both endpoints must support the new peer negotiation; older WebRTC peers must upgrade.

Discovery servers validate the proposed mode with crypto_policy_check_mode() before key exchange, on both TCP and WebSocket listeners. Native discovery clients resolve signaling mode independently of media-peer settings, advertise loaded identities, and retain the signaling crypto context until disconnect. Encrypted signaling includes keepalive packets. The native ACDS connector also accepts a security_policy in its configuration for explicit signaling overrides.

The CLI rejects --encrypt --no-encrypt and --no-auth with any authentication material. The shared policy also rejects these combinations for non-CLI callers. --key --server-key remains valid for mutual authentication. Explicit plaintext TCP/WS connections retain the ENCRYPTION DISABLED notice; TLS/DTLS connections do not produce that misleading warning.

For a future iOS caller, fill crypto_policy_t using the actual connection's transport security and user settings, call crypto_policy_resolve(), and use the returned bitmask in negotiation. Do not infer handshake completion from the encryption bit: AUTH also requires the complete handshake.

Validation:

cmake --build build --target ascii-chat test-crypto-policy
ctest --test-dir build -R '^crypto-policy$' --output-on-failure
python tests/integration/crypto_policy.py /absolute/path/to/ascii-chat
# From web/web, with the rebuilt WASM bundle:
vp dev --config tests/network/crypto-policy.vite.config.ts
# In another terminal:
vp exec node tests/network/crypto-policy-live.mjs /absolute/path/to/ascii-chat http://127.0.0.1:30831

The live browser test records outgoing ACIP packet types, requires a PONG from the native server, and checks wrong-pin/password rejection before CONNECTED. Discovery cases use session-lookup round trips and verify server encryption and identity requirements. Multi-key cases pin the second configured server identity.

WebRTC validation (real native and browser DataChannels):

cmake --build build --target test-webrtc-security
ctest --test-dir build -R '^webrtc-security$' --output-on-failure
python tests/integration/webrtc_security.py /absolute/path/to/ascii-chat
# From web/web:
vp exec playwright test --config tests/e2e/peer-security.config.ts
